what: Aflac sells supplemental insurance: policies that pay cash directly to a person when they are ill or injured, on top of their main health cover. About two-thirds of its profit comes from Japan, where it is the leading cancer insurer.
customers: Employees in Japan and the United States, usually enrolled through their workplace.
money: cancer and medical supplemental policies sold through banks and agencies
accident, disability, dental and critical illness policies sold at the workplace
moat: Decades of brand recognition in Japan, distribution through Japan Post and banks, and a product that competitors have struggled to copy at scale.
risks: Revenue fell about 9% last year as the yen and policy sales weakened
Japan's ageing and shrinking population limits long-term growth
A weak yen reduces reported profit in dollars
Low Japanese interest rates compress investment income
opportunities: Very high profit margins on supplemental policies, about 21% of revenue
Large and consistent buybacks shrink the share count each year
US workplace sales are growing from a smaller base
watch: Sales growth in Japan and the yen exchange rate, which drives reported earnings.
